dbms-intro:0.prompt: Two worker processes append order records to the same CSV file at the same time, and some lines come out interleaved or missing. Which DBMS capability directly addresses this?
options: Data independence between schema levels
Concurrency control through transactions and locking
A declarative query language for reports
Normalisation to remove redundant columns
dbms-intro:0.explanation: A DBMS isolates concurrent writers (locks or MVCC) so each insert is applied whole and none are lost. Normalisation reduces redundancy but does nothing to coordinate simultaneous writes.

dbms-intro:0.prompt: A customer's address is copied into the billing, shipping and CRM files. Support updates it only in the CRM file. What file-system problem is this, and how does a DBMS typically prevent it?
options: Data isolation; the DBMS encrypts each file separately
Redundancy causing inconsistency; store the address once and reference it
Atomicity failure; the DBMS writes all three files in a transaction
Security leak; the DBMS restricts who can read the CRM file
dbms-intro:0.explanation: Duplicated data drifts apart when only one copy is updated. A shared, normalised schema stores the fact once and other tables reference it. Writing three copies atomically would still keep redundant data around.

dbms-intro:0.prompt: A file-based banking script debits account A in one file, then crashes before crediting account B in another file. How does a DBMS prevent this half-finished state?
options: It locks both files so no other process can read them
It logs changes (write-ahead log) and rolls back uncommitted transactions on recovery
It replicates both files to a standby server before writing
It validates balances with CHECK constraints after the crash
dbms-intro:0.explanation: Atomicity comes from logging: on restart the DBMS undoes changes from transactions that never committed, so the debit disappears too. Replication copies the broken state as well, and CHECK constraints can't tell that a transfer was half done.

dbms-intro:0.prompt: In a file-based system, every new business report ("orders over ₹5,000 last month by city") needs a developer to write and deploy a new program. Which DBMS feature removes that bottleneck?
options: A declarative query language such as SQL for ad-hoc queries
Automatic backups taken on a schedule
Storing every table in its own file on disk
Role-based access control for analysts
dbms-intro:0.explanation: With SQL you describe what you want and the optimiser works out how to get it, so new questions don't need new access code. Backups and access control matter, but they don't make data easier to query.

dbms-intro:0.prompt: A video platform stores multi-GB video files. Which design is generally better than putting the raw video bytes in PostgreSQL rows?
options: Store the video in a bytea column and stream it from SQL queries
Store videos in object storage and keep metadata and object keys in the DBMS
Split each video into 1 KB rows so the DBMS can index every chunk
Keep videos in a JSONB column encoded as base64
dbms-intro:0.explanation: Large, immutable, sequentially read blobs fit object storage and CDNs. The DBMS adds value for the queryable, transactional metadata. Huge bytea or base64 values bloat the database, backups and replication without adding anything useful.

dbms-intro:0.prompt: Three different apps write to a shared employees file and each should reject a negative salary. Why is a DBMS CHECK constraint better than validating in each app?
options: CHECK constraints run faster than any application code
The rule is enforced centrally for every writer, including new and buggy ones
Applications are not allowed to validate data once a DBMS is used
CHECK constraints also encrypt the salary column
dbms-intro:0.explanation: An integrity rule declared in the schema applies to every insert and update, whichever app or ad-hoc script sends it. Validating in the app is still good for user feedback, but it can be skipped or implemented inconsistently.

dbms-intro:0.prompt: Support agents should see only tickets for their own region, and never the customers' card_last4 column. Why is this hard with plain files and easier with a DBMS like PostgreSQL?
options: File permissions apply per file, while a DBMS can grant per column and filter rows with row-level security
File systems cannot store more than one region's data in one file
A DBMS encrypts every column automatically so agents can't read it
Files cannot be read by more than one user at a time
dbms-intro:0.explanation: OS permissions are essentially all-or-nothing per file. PostgreSQL supports column-level GRANTs and row-level security policies that filter rows per user. It does not automatically encrypt columns.

dbms-intro:0.prompt: Which file-system problems does a DBMS address by design? Select all that apply.
options: Inconsistency caused by uncontrolled redundancy
Lost updates from concurrent writers
Partial updates left behind after a crash
The need to take backups at all
Reads that are slower than a raw sequential file read
dbms-intro:0.explanation: Central schemas, concurrency control and atomic recovery fix the first three. A DBMS still needs backups (corruption, bad deletes, disasters), and a raw sequential file scan can be faster than going through a DBMS.

dbms-intro:0.prompt: Which are real costs or trade-offs of adopting a DBMS instead of flat files? Select all that apply.
options: Operational work such as tuning, upgrades and monitoring
Per-operation overhead that a tiny embedded workload may not need
Schema changes that need coordinated migrations
Inability to store binary data of any kind
Higher risk of losing committed data on crash
dbms-intro:0.explanation: A DBMS adds operational load, query and transaction overhead, and migration discipline. It can store binary data (e.g. bytea), and durability of committed data after a crash is one of its main strengths, not a weakness.

dbms-intro:0.prompt: SQLite is a DBMS even though it keeps an entire database in a single ordinary file.
options: True
False
dbms-intro:0.explanation: What makes it a DBMS is the software layer: SQL, transactions, constraints and indexing. Where the bytes live doesn't matter. SQLite provides ACID transactions over one file.

dbms-intro:0.prompt: Using a DBMS eliminates all data redundancy.
options: True
False
dbms-intro:0.explanation: A DBMS controls redundancy rather than removing it. Indexes, replicas, materialised views and deliberate denormalisation all duplicate data, but the DBMS keeps those copies consistent or managed.

dbms-intro:1.prompt: What are the three levels of the ANSI/SPARC three-schema architecture?
options: External, conceptual, internal
Client, server, storage
Logical, relational, physical
Presentation, business, data
dbms-intro:1.explanation: External schemas are per-user views, the conceptual schema is the whole logical model (tables, constraints), and the internal schema is physical storage. Presentation/business/data is the three-tier application architecture, a different concept.

dbms-intro:1.prompt: A DBA adds a B-tree index on orders(created_at). No application query changes, but reports run faster. Which property does this show?
options: Logical data independence
Physical data independence
Referential integrity
View serializability
dbms-intro:1.explanation: Indexes belong to the internal (physical) level. Changing them without touching the conceptual schema or queries is physical data independence. Logical independence is about changing the conceptual schema (tables or columns) without breaking external views.

dbms-intro:1.prompt: You split `users` into `users` and `user_profiles`, then create a view named after the old table with the same columns so read queries keep working. Which property does this provide?
options: Physical data independence
Logical data independence
Entity integrity
Transaction isolation
dbms-intro:1.explanation: The conceptual schema changed, and the view (external level) hides the change from applications. That is logical data independence. Physical independence would cover storage changes such as indexes or tablespaces.

dbms-intro:1.prompt: A DBA moves a large table to a tablespace on faster SSDs. Which schema level changes?
options: External
Conceptual
Internal
All three levels
dbms-intro:1.explanation: Where and how data is stored is the internal schema. Table definitions (conceptual) and views (external) are unchanged, so applications don't notice.

dbms-intro:1.prompt: Why is logical data independence generally harder to achieve than physical data independence?
options: Physical changes always require downtime while logical ones don't
Applications depend directly on the logical structure, and views can't hide every change
Logical changes are made by developers, who don't use views
Only the internal level has a mapping to the level above it
dbms-intro:1.explanation: Queries name tables and columns, so removing a column or changing its meaning can break them, and compatibility views may be read-only. Physical changes sit under a stable logical interface. Both levels have mappings.

dbms-intro:1.prompt: In PostgreSQL, which object most directly implements an external schema for a reporting team?
options: A tablespace
A view exposing only the columns and rows they need
A B-tree index on the reporting columns
A WAL archive
dbms-intro:1.explanation: External schemas are tailored user views of the data, which SQL views (plus grants) provide. Tablespaces, indexes and WAL are all internal-level storage concerns.

dbms-intro:1.prompt: In PostgreSQL 16, the compatibility view `users` is defined as a JOIN of `accounts` and `user_profiles`. Old code runs `UPDATE users SET bio = 'x' WHERE id = 1`. What happens?
options: PostgreSQL rewrites it to update user_profiles automatically
It errors unless you add an INSTEAD OF trigger (or rule) on the view
It silently updates nothing and reports UPDATE 0
It updates both base tables in one implicit transaction
dbms-intro:1.explanation: PostgreSQL automatically makes only simple single-table views updatable. A view over a join can't be updated unless an INSTEAD OF trigger tells PostgreSQL how to apply the change. This is a common limit of logical data independence.

dbms-intro:1.prompt: Which changes are internal-level (physical) changes that shouldn't require changing application SQL? Select all that apply.
options: Adding a B-tree index
Changing a table's fillfactor
Moving a table to another tablespace
Renaming a column
Dropping a column
dbms-intro:1.explanation: Indexes, page fill settings and tablespaces only affect storage and access paths. Renaming or dropping a column changes the conceptual schema, and queries that reference it break.

dbms-intro:1.prompt: Which practices help applications survive conceptual-schema changes (better logical data independence)? Select all that apply.
options: Listing columns explicitly instead of SELECT *
Giving consumers views or an API instead of raw tables
Expand-and-contract migrations (add new, backfill, then remove old)
Reading result columns by ordinal position
Letting several services query each other's tables directly
dbms-intro:1.explanation: Explicit columns, stable interfaces and staged migrations keep consumers working while the schema changes. Relying on column positions or sharing tables between services ties every consumer to the current shape of the tables.

dbms-intro:1.prompt: Physical data independence means you can change how data is stored (files, indexes, storage devices) without rewriting application queries.
options: True
False
dbms-intro:1.explanation: That is the definition: the conceptual/internal mapping absorbs storage changes, so queries written against tables keep working.

dbms-intro:1.prompt: The conceptual schema describes how records are laid out in pages and blocks on disk.
options: True
False
dbms-intro:1.explanation: Page and block layout is the internal schema. The conceptual schema describes entities, attributes, relationships and constraints for the whole database, independent of storage.

dbms-intro:2.prompt: An Employee entity has date_of_birth, and age is always computed from it. In ER terms, what is age?
options: A composite attribute
A multivalued attribute
A derived attribute
A key attribute
dbms-intro:2.explanation: A derived attribute's value is computed from other stored attributes (shown as a dashed ellipse). Composite means it has sub-parts, which age doesn't.

dbms-intro:2.prompt: A Customer's address consists of street, city and pincode. What kind of attribute is address?
options: Simple
Composite
Derived
Multivalued
dbms-intro:2.explanation: A composite attribute can be split into meaningful sub-attributes. It would be multivalued only if a customer could have several addresses.

dbms-intro:2.prompt: A student can have any number of phone numbers. How is this attribute classified, and how is it usually mapped to tables?
options: Composite; phone1, phone2 and phone3 columns
Multivalued; a separate student_phones(student_id, phone) table
Derived; computed from the contacts table at query time
Simple; one comma-separated text column
dbms-intro:2.explanation: Several values of the same attribute per entity is multivalued, and the standard mapping is a child table keyed by (owner id, value). Fixed phone1..3 columns cap the count and leave NULLs.

dbms-intro:2.prompt: A developer wants to add an `age` integer column next to `date_of_birth` in the users table. What is the main problem?
options: Integers can't store ages above 127
Age changes every year, so the stored value goes stale unless something keeps updating it
PostgreSQL forbids two date-related columns in one table
It creates a composite key that slows down inserts
dbms-intro:2.explanation: Storing a derived, time-dependent value creates an inconsistency risk: it's correct only on the day it was written. Compute it at query time (e.g. in a view) from date_of_birth. A PostgreSQL integer easily holds any age.

dbms-intro:2.prompt: In PostgreSQL 16 you try `age int GENERATED ALWAYS AS (date_part('year', age(current_date, dob))) STORED`. What happens?
options: It works and is recomputed automatically every day
It fails because generation expressions must be immutable, and current_date isn't
It works but is only recomputed when the row is read
It fails because generated columns can't be integers
dbms-intro:2.explanation: Stored generated columns are computed on write and must use only immutable functions. current_date changes over time, so PostgreSQL rejects it. Compute age in a view or at query time instead.

dbms-intro:2.prompt: Posts store tags as a single text column like 'node,sql,redis'. Finding all posts tagged 'sql' is slow and sometimes matches 'nosql'. What is the underlying modelling mistake?
options: Tags should be a derived attribute computed from the post body
A multivalued attribute was packed into one non-atomic column instead of a separate table
Tags should be a composite attribute split into tag1, tag2, tag3
The column needs a CHECK constraint on its length
dbms-intro:2.explanation: Tags are multivalued. Packing them into a string breaks atomicity, which forces LIKE scans with false matches. A post_tags(post_id, tag_id) table gives exact, indexable lookups. Fixed tag1..3 columns just move the problem.

dbms-intro:2.prompt: Should Department be an attribute of Employee or its own entity, when departments have a budget and a manager and are shared by many employees?
options: An attribute, because each employee belongs to one department
Its own entity, because it has its own attributes and is shared
A derived attribute computed from the manager
A multivalued attribute of Employee
dbms-intro:2.explanation: Once something has properties of its own and many instances refer to it, model it as an entity linked by a relationship. As an attribute, the budget and manager would be repeated on every employee row.

dbms-intro:2.prompt: In PostgreSQL, you store a product's multivalued category_ids as an integer[] array instead of a junction table. What is a real trade-off?
options: Arrays can't be indexed, so every lookup is a full scan
A GIN index supports containment queries, but elements can't have foreign key constraints
Arrays are limited to 10 elements per row
Arrays are not allowed in tables that have a primary key
dbms-intro:2.explanation: GIN indexes make queries like `category_ids @> '{5}'` fast, but PostgreSQL has no per-element foreign keys, so deleted categories can leave dangling ids. A junction table keeps referential integrity.

dbms-intro:2.prompt: Which of these are typically derived attributes? Select all that apply.
options: An order's total, from its line items
A person's age, from date of birth
A department's employee count
A customer's email address
A product's SKU
dbms-intro:2.explanation: Totals, ages and counts can be computed from other stored data. Email and SKU are base facts that nothing else determines. Teams sometimes store derived values for speed, but then they must be kept in sync.

dbms-intro:2.prompt: Which designs let you filter customers by city efficiently in PostgreSQL? Select all that apply.
options: A flattened address_city column with a B-tree index
A separate addresses table with an indexed city column
A JSONB address with an expression index on (address->>'city')
One free-text address column queried with LIKE '%Pune%'
dbms-intro:2.explanation: Flattening, normalising and an expression index on JSONB all give an indexable city value. A leading-wildcard LIKE on free text can't use a B-tree index and also matches 'Pune' anywhere in the address, such as street names.

dbms-intro:2.prompt: In Chen notation, a multivalued attribute is drawn as a double ellipse and a derived attribute as a dashed ellipse.
options: True
False
dbms-intro:2.explanation: These are the standard Chen ER conventions. Key attributes are underlined, and composite attributes branch into their component ellipses.

dbms-intro:3.prompt: Students enrol in many courses and each course has many students. How is this relationship represented in tables?
options: A course_id column in students
A student_id column in courses
A junction table enrollments(student_id, course_id)
An array of course ids in students with no constraints
dbms-intro:3.explanation: Many-to-many needs a separate relation whose rows pair one student with one course, with both foreign keys. A single FK column on either side can hold only one value per row.

dbms-intro:3.prompt: "Every employee must belong to a department" is total participation of Employee in WorksIn. How is it usually enforced when employees.dept_id is the FK?
options: Make employees.dept_id NOT NULL
Add a UNIQUE constraint on employees.dept_id
Make departments.id a composite key
Add ON DELETE CASCADE to departments
dbms-intro:3.explanation: Total participation means no employee can exist without a department, so the FK must not be NULL. UNIQUE would wrongly limit each department to one employee.

dbms-intro:3.prompt: Users and passports are 1:1. Every passport belongs to a user, but most users don't have a passport. Where should the foreign key go?
options: users.passport_id, nullable
passports.user_id NOT NULL UNIQUE
A junction table with no constraints
Both tables, each referencing the other
dbms-intro:3.explanation: Putting the FK on the side with total participation avoids NULLs, and UNIQUE keeps it 1:1. A nullable users.passport_id works but leaves NULL on most rows. Mutual FKs complicate inserts and deletes.

dbms-intro:3.prompt: "A supplier supplies a part to a project" relates Supplier, Part and Project together in one fact. What is the degree of this relationship?
options: Unary
Binary
Ternary
Quaternary
dbms-intro:3.explanation: Three entity sets take part in each relationship instance, so it is ternary (degree 3). Degree counts participating entity sets, not cardinality.

dbms-intro:3.prompt: Why can't the ternary Supplies(supplier, part, project) generally be replaced by three binary relationships (supplier–part, part–project, supplier–project)?
options: Binary relationships can't have foreign keys
The binaries lose which supplier supplied which part to which project
Three binary tables always use more storage than one ternary table
ER diagrams don't allow more than two binary relationships per entity
dbms-intro:3.explanation: If S1 supplies P1 (to some project), P1 goes to J1 and S1 supplies J1, it doesn't follow that S1 supplied P1 to J1. Joining the binaries can create spurious combinations. Storage size isn't the issue.

dbms-intro:3.prompt: Each employee may have a manager, who is also an employee. How is this recursive (unary) relationship mapped?
options: A separate managers table copying employee columns
A nullable manager_id column in employees referencing employees(id)
A composite primary key (id, manager_id)
A CHECK constraint listing valid manager ids
dbms-intro:3.explanation: A self-referencing FK models a 1:N recursive relationship. It's nullable because the top manager has none. A copied managers table duplicates people who are both employee and manager.

dbms-intro:3.prompt: Rule: every department must have at least one employee, with FK employees.dept_id → departments.id. How can PostgreSQL enforce this side of the participation?
options: Make departments.id NOT NULL
A plain FK can't; use a deferred constraint trigger (or app logic) checked at commit
Add ON DELETE RESTRICT to employees.dept_id
Add UNIQUE to employees.dept_id
dbms-intro:3.explanation: FKs enforce 'the child points to an existing parent', not 'the parent has at least one child'. You need a check that runs after both rows exist, such as a DEFERRABLE constraint trigger. RESTRICT only stops deleting referenced departments.

dbms-intro:3.prompt: Which of these relationships need their own junction table when mapped to relations? Select all that apply.
options: Students–Courses (many-to-many)
Actors–Movies (many-to-many)
Supplier–Part–Project (ternary)
User–Orders (one-to-many)
User–Profile (one-to-one)
dbms-intro:3.explanation: M:N and ternary relationships can't fit in one FK column, so they get their own table. 1:N puts the FK on the many side, and 1:1 puts a unique FK on one side.

dbms-intro:3.prompt: The Enrolls relationship has an attribute `grade`. Which statements about placing relationship attributes are correct? Select all that apply.
options: For M:N, the attribute goes in the junction table
For 1:N, it can move to the table on the N side
For M:N, it must go in the student table
For 1:1, it can go in either participating table
dbms-intro:3.explanation: A grade belongs to a (student, course) pair, so in M:N it lives with the pair. In 1:N each N-side row has at most one partner, and in 1:1 either side works. The student table would need one grade column per course.

dbms-intro:3.prompt: A one-to-many relationship is implemented by putting the foreign key in the table on the 'many' side.
options: True
False
dbms-intro:3.explanation: Each many-side row references its single parent (e.g. orders.user_id). Putting it on the 'one' side would need multiple values per row.

dbms-intro:3.prompt: If an entity has total participation in a relationship, the relationship must be one-to-one.
options: True
False
dbms-intro:3.explanation: Participation (must every instance take part?) and cardinality (how many partners?) are independent. Every order must have a customer (total), but a customer can have many orders (1:N).

dbms-intro:4.prompt: What defines a weak entity set?
options: It has no attributes other than a foreign key
It has no key of its own and is identified by its owner's key plus a partial key
Its rows are deleted automatically after a timeout
It participates in only one relationship
dbms-intro:4.explanation: A weak entity depends on an identifying (owner) entity. Its discriminator is unique only within one owner. It can have other attributes; what's missing is a key of its own.

dbms-intro:4.prompt: Which of these is the best example of a weak entity?
options: A User identified by a UUID
A Room numbered 101, unique only within its Building
A Product identified by a global SKU
A Country identified by its ISO code
dbms-intro:4.explanation: Room 101 exists in many buildings, so a room is identified only together with its building. The others have globally unique identifiers and are strong entities.

dbms-intro:4.prompt: How do you map the weak entity OrderLine(line_no, qty), owned by Order(id), to a table?
options: order_lines(line_no PK, qty) with no reference to orders
order_lines(order_id FK, line_no, qty) with PRIMARY KEY (order_id, line_no)
order_lines(id SERIAL PK, qty), with line_no stored in orders
Add line_no and qty columns directly to the orders table
dbms-intro:4.explanation: The weak entity's key is the owner's key plus its partial key, and the owner FK usually has ON DELETE CASCADE. line_no alone repeats across orders, so it can't be the primary key on its own.

dbms-intro:4.prompt: A designer notices Car and Truck share registration_no, make and model, so creates a Vehicle superclass. What is this process called?
options: Specialization
Generalization
Aggregation
Normalization
dbms-intro:4.explanation: Generalization is bottom-up: common features of existing entity sets are pulled into a superclass. Specialization is top-down: starting from Vehicle and defining subclasses.

dbms-intro:4.prompt: A Person can be both a Student and an Employee at the same university. What constraint applies to this specialization?
options: Disjoint
Overlapping
Partial and disjoint
Weak
dbms-intro:4.explanation: Overlapping means one superclass instance can belong to several subclasses. Disjoint would force each person to be either a student or an employee, not both.

dbms-intro:4.prompt: Payment has subtypes Card and UPI, each with 2–3 extra columns, and most queries list all payments together. Which mapping fits best?
options: Single table: payments with a type column and nullable subtype columns
A separate table per subtype with no shared parent table
An EAV table of (payment_id, attribute_name, value)
One database per subtype
dbms-intro:4.explanation: With few subtype columns and many cross-type queries, one table avoids joins and UNIONs. Use CHECK constraints to tie subtype columns to the type. Per-subtype tables make 'list all payments' a UNION, and EAV loses typing and constraints.

dbms-intro:4.prompt: You map a Vehicle hierarchy as concrete table-per-subclass (cars and trucks tables, no vehicles table). What problem appears when a `rentals` table must reference any vehicle?
options: Cars and trucks can't have primary keys
A single foreign key can't reference either table, and ids may collide across them
Queries on cars alone become slower than with a single table
PostgreSQL limits each database to one table per entity type
dbms-intro:4.explanation: An FK targets exactly one table, so 'any vehicle' needs nullable FKs to both tables or a polymorphic id with no integrity. Separate sequences can also issue the same id twice. A parent vehicles table (class-table mapping) solves this.

dbms-intro:4.prompt: Which statements about weak entities are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The weak entity has total participation in its identifying relationship
Its partial key (discriminator) is drawn with a dashed underline
It can exist without an owner entity
Its table's primary key includes the owner's primary key
It can't have attributes besides the partial key
dbms-intro:4.explanation: A weak entity always needs its owner, the discriminator gets a dashed underline in Chen notation, and the mapped primary key is (owner key, discriminator). It can have any number of other attributes.

dbms-intro:4.prompt: Single-table mapping in PostgreSQL: vehicles(kind, seats, payload_tons, …). Business rule: every vehicle is exactly a car or a truck (total, disjoint). Which constraints help enforce it? Select all that apply.
options: kind NOT NULL with CHECK (kind IN ('car', 'truck'))
A CHECK requiring seats only for cars and payload_tons only for trucks
A foreign key from a cars table to vehicles
A UNIQUE constraint on the kind column
dbms-intro:4.explanation: A non-null discriminator restricted to the two subtypes enforces total and disjoint, and a per-kind CHECK keeps the subtype columns consistent. An FK from cars doesn't force every vehicle to have a subtype, and UNIQUE on kind would allow only one car.

dbms-intro:4.prompt: Specialization is the top-down process of defining subclasses of an entity set based on distinguishing characteristics.
options: True
False
dbms-intro:4.explanation: Specialization starts from a general entity (Employee) and defines subclasses (Engineer, Manager). Generalization goes the other way, bottom-up.

dbms-intro:4.prompt: In an overlapping specialization, each superclass instance belongs to at most one subclass.
options: True
False
dbms-intro:4.explanation: 'At most one subclass' describes a disjoint specialization. Overlapping lets an instance belong to several subclasses, such as a person who is both a student and an employee.

dbms-intro:5.prompt: How is a strong entity set with simple attributes mapped to the relational model?
options: A table with one column per simple attribute and the entity key as the primary key
One table per attribute, joined by a shared id
A single JSON column holding all attributes
A view over the tables of related entities
dbms-intro:5.explanation: Each strong entity becomes a relation whose columns are its simple (or flattened composite) attributes, with the key as primary key. One table per attribute is a needlessly fragmented design.

dbms-intro:5.prompt: How is the M:N relationship Authors–Books mapped?
options: A nullable author_id column in books
book_authors(author_id FK, book_id FK) with PRIMARY KEY (author_id, book_id)
Merge authors and books into one table
A book_ids text column in authors
dbms-intro:5.explanation: M:N becomes its own relation with FKs to both sides, and the pair is the key so duplicate links are impossible. A single author_id in books supports only one author per book.

dbms-intro:5.prompt: Customer 1:N Order has a relationship attribute placed_via ('web' or 'app'). Where does placed_via go in the tables?
options: In the customers table
In the orders table, next to customer_id
In a separate customer_orders junction table only
In a lookup table keyed by customer
dbms-intro:5.explanation: In 1:N, each order relates to exactly one customer, so the relationship's attributes move to the N side along with the FK. In the customers table there would be one value per customer instead of one per order.

dbms-intro:5.prompt: Employee has a multivalued attribute skills. What is the standard mapping?
options: employee_skills(employee_id FK, skill) with PRIMARY KEY (employee_id, skill)
skill1, skill2 and skill3 columns in employees
A comma-separated skills column
A skills table with employee_name as primary key
dbms-intro:5.explanation: Each value becomes a row in a child table keyed by owner plus value, which allows any number of skills and prevents duplicates. Numbered columns cap the count and make 'who has SQL?' a multi-column search.

dbms-intro:5.prompt: The ER model shows Order.total as a derived attribute (sum of line items). What is the usual default when mapping to tables?
options: Always store it as a column updated by the app
Don't store it; compute it in queries or a view, and denormalise only if measurements show the need
Store it in a separate totals table keyed by total
Represent it as a multivalued attribute table
dbms-intro:5.explanation: Derived values are normally computed to avoid inconsistency. Storing one is a deliberate denormalisation for performance that then needs triggers or careful updates. Storing it by default invites drift.

dbms-intro:5.prompt: Person and PersonDetails are 1:1 with total participation on both sides, and they are always read together. What mapping is usually best?
options: Two tables, each with a foreign key to the other
Merge them into a single table
A junction table linking person and details ids
Two tables with no foreign key, joined on name
dbms-intro:5.explanation: When every person has exactly one details row and they're read together, a separate table adds a join and mutual-FK insert problems for no benefit. Splitting only makes sense for very wide, rarely read, or differently secured columns.

dbms-intro:5.prompt: A ternary relationship Supplies(supplier, part, project) has the constraint that each (project, part) pair has exactly one supplier. What should the primary key of the supplies table be?
options: (supplier_id, part_id, project_id)
(project_id, part_id)
(supplier_id)
A surrogate id with no other unique constraint
dbms-intro:5.explanation: The constraint says (project, part) determines the supplier, so that pair is the minimal key. Using all three columns would allow two suppliers for the same pair. A bare surrogate id enforces nothing.

dbms-intro:5.prompt: Users can follow other users (M:N recursive relationship). Which table design is correct?
options: A followers int[] column in users with no constraints
follows(follower_id FK→users, followee_id FK→users) with PRIMARY KEY (follower_id, followee_id)
A follow_count column in users
follows(user_id PK, followed_user_id)
dbms-intro:5.explanation: A recursive M:N relationship is still M:N: a junction table with two FKs to the same table, with the pair as key. Optionally add CHECK (follower_id <> followee_id). Making user_id the PK would let each user follow only one person.

dbms-intro:5.prompt: Mapping Student M:N Course with relationship attribute grade. Which columns belong in the enrollments table? Select all that apply.
options: student_id (FK to students)
course_id (FK to courses)
grade
course_title
student_name
dbms-intro:5.explanation: The junction table holds both keys plus attributes of the relationship itself. course_title and student_name describe the entities and already live in their own tables; copying them here causes update anomalies.

dbms-intro:5.prompt: users 1:1 profiles is mapped with a profiles.user_id column, and every profile must belong to a user. Which constraints are needed to enforce this faithfully? Select all that apply.
options: FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id)
UNIQUE (or PRIMARY KEY) on profiles.user_id
NOT NULL on profiles.user_id
An extra index on users.id
CHECK (user_id > 0)
dbms-intro:5.explanation: The FK makes it reference a real user, UNIQUE stops one user having two profiles (which would make it 1:N), and NOT NULL forces each profile to have an owner. users.id is already indexed as the PK, and a positivity check adds nothing.

dbms-intro:5.prompt: In PostgreSQL, you can map an M:N relationship as an integer[] column of foreign ids in one table and still have the database enforce referential integrity for each element.
options: True
False
dbms-intro:5.explanation: PostgreSQL has no foreign keys on array elements, so deleted parents leave dangling ids unless you add triggers. A junction table with real FKs is the standard mapping.
